bme-y11-u1-misleading-and-deceptive-cond.title: The overall impression of a claim

blocks.text: Australian consumer law prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct in trade or commerce. Examine the overall impression made on the relevant audience, including words, pictures, omissions and qualifications.
A statement can mislead without an intention to deceive. Small print cannot contradict the main message of an advertisement.
Bait advertising concerns an advertised offer without reasonable availability in the relevant circumstances. Clearly disclosed limits and the actual offer matter.
A scientific claim should have a sound evidential basis. A business should not invent test results, overstate what research shows or imply an endorsement that does not exist.
Country-of-origin claims must be accurate and supported. Distinguish the origin of ingredients, the place of manufacture and the wording of a particular claim.

Example: a food business should check its sourcing and processing evidence before describing a product as Australian-made. Evaluate the actual representation rather than assuming a familiar brand or flag proves origin.
Consumer guarantees are automatic legal protections for qualifying purchases. An optional warranty is an additional promise and does not remove those guarantees.
Mandatory safety standards apply to specified products. An Australian Standard is not automatically compulsory merely because it exists; check whether a legal requirement makes it mandatory.

The remedy depends on the problem and applicable law. A major product failure generally gives the consumer a choice between refund and replacement. A minor problem that can be remedied ordinarily gives the supplier an opportunity to fix it within a reasonable time.
A change of mind differs from a failure to meet a consumer guarantee. A store policy cannot remove statutory rights by displaying a blanket “no refunds” notice.
Identify the product or service, the guarantee involved, the nature of the problem and the appropriate remedy. Keep evidence such as proof of purchase and communications.

Example: a newly purchased appliance that is unsafe may involve a major failure. A small repairable fault may require a different response. Explain why the classification matters rather than offering the same remedy for every complaint.

A business’ public image is the business is perceived by the community and the reputation it has.
This is created by the ideas and opinions that the general public holds about that business.
These ideas and opinions are shaped by what the business does, and is seen doing, in the eye of the general public.
Some brands have spent years cultivating excellent public image, while others have to continue to work on their public image to remain successful!

High business competition means that businesses need to compete for consumers attention, loyalty and dollar!
Where a business has a positive public image, this can attract higher consumer loyalty, greater market share and more sales.
On the other hand, a negative public image can greatly harm business sales and a business's ability to compete in the market.

Corporate Social responsibility is a moral obligation on a business to make decisions and take actions that are beneficial to society as a whole.

Do good stuff! Publicly. Then talk about it, a lot. Over and over again. (positive Public Relations)
Options:
Give ‘Green Gifts’
Donate to Charities / Causes
Provide Excellent Service (consistently)
Behave ethically
Corporate Sponsorship

Businesses may choose to give their consumers branded green gifts for shopping with them including reusable shopping bags, water bottles and stationery.
They get extra points if they've made these things out of recycled materials!
This demonstrates the business's commitment to sustainability and aligns business values with consumer preferences.

Giving to charities is another great way that businesses can show their philanthropic side.
They usually give to charities that will resonate with their target audience.
Perhaps they are Mum's? Then they might donate to Save the Children.
Perhaps they are millennials, then they might decide to donate to an ocean plastic clean-up cause etc….

Providing excellent service travels like wildfire!
This is an excellent way of encouraging word of mouth promotion, simply by treating a customer's better than the competitor to do…
Maybe a company would provide an easy to use with platform to use their service, or follow up to see how your new product is suiting you?

Most consumers love a do-gooder.
Brands that decide to treat customers and suppliers honestly and with integrity will always be more successful than those that try to exploit.
Think about stuff like:
Cruelty to animals
Child labour
Waste products
Local community exploitation

Corporate sponsorship is another option to promote a brand's positive public image and align it with that of another much-loved business/event (“image transfer”).
This is not the same as donating to a charity as it is a business agreement that is paid for, whereby both businesses benefit.
Corporate sponsorship is particularly useful in increasing consumer salience and recall. Importantly, the act of sponsoring a business/event reveals the business’ values.

Benefits of corporate sponsorship include:
Brand Visibility (seen by lots of potential customers)
Positioning (alignment of values)
Publicity (promotion and being ‘thanked’ as the major sponsor)
Market Reach (targeting the same customers)

Businesses need to be very cautious of the role that they play in contributing to, and repairing, environmental issues about the planet because…consumers care!

Businesses are interested in environmental issues because this is a way that they can show they share the same values as their customers.
higher consumer loyalty
greater market share
more sales

Businesses can strengthen their positive public image, by actively taking environmentally conscious actions, and reducing their impact on the planet.
This can include taking action on:
Climate change
Pollution
Energy Use
Animal Testing

Businesses are ‘going green’ and responding to environmental issues by doing things like:
Offering customers Carbon Offsets
Recycling waste or producing products from recycled waste
Using Renewable Energy sources
Investing in reforestation initiatives

UK-based company
Brands like Ben & Jerry’s, Dove, Lipton, etc.
Twenty-six of Unilever’s brands are 100% sourced from sustainable materials
Lofty goal of halving its environmental footprint and becoming carbon negative by 2030.
Adopting a Sustainable Agriculture Code in 2018 (only sourcing raw materials from global suppliers in ecologically sustainable ways)
Reduced CO2 emissions by 65%, and its total waste sent for disposal by 96%, compared to 2008 levels.
Reusable and recyclable packaging (partnership with Loop).

Businesses contribute to climate change through pollution. this is measured by a carbon footprint.
The carbon footprint includes the emissions produced when he good or service is created as well as when it is consumed.
Consumers expect businesses to be taking action to minimise their contribution to climate change.
If consumers can see businesses taking ethical actions to support and preserve the environment, this will improve a business's public image.

Pollution control is when businesses clean up contaminants they create (an environmental management process) e.g. treating wastewater before it is released into the local environment.
Problem? It’s a reactive solution, the waste has already been produced.
Pollution prevention is much better, though both responses require investment which reduces the number of businesses who decide to take this on ($$$).

All businesses require energy to produce their goods and services.
Reducing energy usage can both decrease environmental impact and reduce expenses.
Examples include energy efficient lighting, using natural light instead, incorporating renewable energy, switching off machines computers and lighting when not in use, upgrading all the equipment to more energy efficient equipment etc…

Businesses must test products such as cosmetics, medicines, shampoos and household cleaners on animals before they are allowed to sell them to consumers.
Australia has banned cosmetic testing on animals but many products sold here, contain ingredients tested on animals in other places.
This is associated with animal cruelty and can be very bad for public image. On the other hand, businesses that promote their decision not to test on animals can be very good for business!

These alternatives to animal testing include:
tests using human cells and tissues (also known as in vitro methods)
advanced computer-modeling techniques (often referred to as in silico models)
studies with human volunteers

Greenwashing is the process of appearing to be environmentally committed, but actually having nothing to backup these claims.
Greenwashing is everywhere in our supermarkets and are shops!
Consumers can see through many greenwashing attempts, but many of them are highly successful.

Volkswagen admitted to cheating emissions tests by fitting various vehicles with a “defect” device, with software that could detect when it was undergoing an emissions test and altering the performance to reduce the emissions level.
Emissions were 40 times higher than U.S. standards permitted.
$30 billion in fines and damages
Brand was damaged, huge fines threatened its survival, VW officials were caught lying, and VW’s CEO Martin Winterkorn resigned.

Swedish company Hennes & Mauritz Group
H&M “Conscious” Collection (launched 2010)
Products labeled as "sustainable" sell much faster than regular products
Made from at least 50% sustainably sourced materials – like organic cotton and recycled polyester
One top is composed of 95% cotton and 5% spandex, and only the outer layer of the top contains 25% recycled cotton…
The sustainability report states that of all the materials H&M uses, just 0.7% are recycled.
In 2019, the Norwegian consumer authority pilloried H&M and called the company's behavior "misleading" for consumers.

A contract generally requires intention to create legal relations, agreement through offer and acceptance, and consideration exchanged between the parties. Identify what each party promises and when an offer is accepted.
A quotation or advertisement is not automatically a binding offer in every situation. Apply the facts rather than assuming every conversation creates a contract.

Capacity concerns whether a party can enter an enforceable agreement. Minors and some other parties can raise special issues, so it is too broad to say every agreement involving a person under eighteen is automatically void.

Consent must be genuine. Misrepresentation, duress and undue influence can affect enforceability. The agreement must have a lawful purpose. Certain transactions also have writing or other formal requirements.
A supplier offers a café a specified quantity of beans at an agreed price and delivery date. The café accepts. The parties intend a commercial relationship and exchange goods and payment.

Before concluding that the contract is enforceable, consider the parties’ capacity, whether consent was genuine and whether the purpose and any required formalities are lawful. A clear written record can reduce disputes.

The NES establishes a minimum entitlement framework for employees in the national workplace relations system. Awards, enterprise agreements and employment contracts cannot exclude applicable NES protections. Some entitlements vary by employment type and eligibility.

Minimum pay and unfair-dismissal protection are related employment-law topics, but should not be described as separate NES entitlements. Western Australia also has a state industrial relations system; check which system covers the employment.

NES areas include maximum weekly hours, flexible working arrangements, casual employment pathways, parental leave, annual leave, personal/carer’s and compassionate leave, family and domestic violence leave, community service leave, long service leave, public holidays, superannuation contributions, and notice/redundancy and information-statement requirements.

For each area, connect the entitlement to a business responsibility. For example, rostering must accommodate applicable hours and leave requirements. Use the current Fair Work list to confirm the detailed grouping and eligibility.

An award sets minimum pay and conditions for a particular industry or occupation. An enterprise agreement applies to a workplace or group of workplaces. The National Minimum Wage provides a safety net for relevant award/agreement-free employees.

Rates change and can vary for juniors, apprentices, trainees and some supported employment arrangements. Use the current Fair Work pay information for rates. The earlier dollar figure is not retained as a current rate.
Unfair dismissal generally concerns a dismissal that is harsh, unjust or unreasonable, subject to statutory eligibility and exclusions. The Fair Work Commission determines applications.

The minimum employment period is generally six months, or twelve months for a small-business employer, with other conditions also applying. Genuine redundancy and the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code can affect a case. A business should use a valid process and keep appropriate records.
